title: Getting a file into the running TUI, on all three platforms
separate_from: The seven interpretation sub-cases in a10.key.json. Understanding a PDF and receiving a PDF are different capabilities. A backend test that parses a document must never be counted as evidence that dropping one into the TUI works, least of all on Windows, where the path is the part that breaks.
user_outcome: A person has the TUI open, drags a file onto the terminal window or pastes its path, and the assistant can see what is in the file.
setup: python3 gen/gen_a10_tui_attach.py --out <a scratch dir>. Twelve artifacts across four directories.
why_a_canary: Each artifact contains a token that appears in the file and nowhere in its name or its path. The generator asserts this. So a reply containing the token proves the bytes were read; a reply that echoes the path, guesses from the file name, or describes what the file is probably about cannot produce it.

locations.role: the control. If this fails the feature is simply broken; the quoting cases below tell you nothing further.
a directory with a space in it

an apostrophe and double quotes in a directory name. A double quote is not legal in a Windows file name, so Windows gets the apostrophe-only variant -- the apostrophe is the character that actually breaks shell quoting, and it is present everywhere.

how_to_run_it.rule: Drive the real TUI the way a person would. Do not call an attachment API, do not pass the file on the command line, and do not pre-load it into a session file. If the only way to get the file in is a route no user would find, that is a FAIL with a note, not a pass.
how_to_run_it.macos: Open the TUI in Terminal.app and drag the file from Finder onto the window. Finder inserts the path with spaces backslash-escaped. Also try pasting the path in quotes.
how_to_run_it.windows: Open the TUI in Windows Terminal and drag the file from Explorer. Explorer inserts the path wrapped in double quotes with backslash separators. Also try a path typed without quotes, and one under a directory whose name contains a space.
how_to_run_it.linux: Drag from the file manager into the terminal. Most send a file:// URI rather than a plain path. Also try a plain absolute path.
how_to_run_it.prompt: After the path is in the input, send: "What token is written inside this file?"

matrix: 4 locations x 3 file types x 3 platforms = 36 cells. Record every cell. A platform is only PASS when all 12 of its cells pass.
pass_condition: For each cell: the assistant's reply contains that artifact's canary token exactly.
fail_condition: FAIL for a cell if the reply does not contain the canary. That includes every one of these, which are the shapes this actually breaks in: the TUI shows the dropped path as plain text and nothing is attached; the reply says the file cannot be found; the reply describes the file from its name without reading it; the path is truncated at the first space; the backslashes are eaten as escape characters; the non-ASCII directory comes through as mojibake and the open fails. FAIL also if the TUI crashes, hangs, or corrupts the input line when the path is dropped.
not_a_pass: An answer that names the file correctly, or explains that it would need the file, is a FAIL. The user's file was on their screen and the product did not read it.
unproven_condition: UNPROVEN only if no interactive terminal is available on that host, since drag-and-drop cannot be simulated without one. A headless approximation is not this row and must not be recorded as this row.
na_condition: N/A for a platform only if the product does not claim to run there. Wayland Core claims Linux, macOS and Windows, so no platform here is N/A.
